anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The log-writer path (log buffer, log files, archive/replication pipeline) becomes the bottleneck, inflating commit and log-flush latency.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer saturates its IOPS/MB-per-s capacity, driving up read-write latencies and queue depths for all database files.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, asynchronous-I/O contexts, shared memory, or process threads are reached, preventing the database from issuing or completing additional I/O or spawning helper tasks.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database experiences compound symptoms: commit operations stall behind saturated log devices whose writes themselves wait in deep OS-level I/O queues; data and log read/write latencies climb simultaneously, obscuring whether slowness originates in the engine or the device; background tasks such as checkpoint, archiver, and replication sender processes intermittently fail to open new log segments or allocate AIO contexts, producing error bursts in both database and system logs; queue build-up in the log subsystem triggers frequent checkpoints and aggressive log switches, which further inflate I/O pressure on an already bandwidth-starved storage array; overall throughput collapses while CPU remains under-utilised and sessions time out.

Causally, log-heavy OLTP traffic generates sustained redo that must be flushed. The undersized or co-located log files hit the physical throughput ceiling of the shared storage, lengthening sync times. As waits accumulate, the database spawns more helper processes and AIO requests, quickly consuming kernel file-handle and AIO limits. Once those limits are breached, new I/O submissions are throttled or fail, forcing the engine to fall back to synchronous, single-threaded or buffered I/O, which further degrades throughput and amplifies storage congestion. The persistent storage backlog, in turn, keeps log segments open longer, blocks checkpoints, and inflates recovery-related disk activity, creating a feedback loop that deepens the performance crisis and can escalate into a full write stall or service outage.

entry.official_definition: Controls how long STOP REPLICA waits before timing out.
entry.trigger_condition: A STOP REPLICA administrative operation waits longer than rpl_stop_replica_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The administrative replication stop operation times out.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL replication system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when replication endpoints stop exchanging or applying data within the configured timeout window, causing the channel to be considered inactive.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect replication channel health, sender/receiver status, upstream and downstream connectivity, and whether lag or stalled apply is preventing timely progress.
